title: UX Is Thankless (That's Good)
intro: UX work feels thankless because people adapt to improvements and forget what came before. Hedonic adaptation explains it — and makes it a sign of success rather than a problem.

learn.title: What hedonic adaptation is
learn.text:
The human tendency to **return to a stable level of satisfaction after something changes**. A positive change feels meaningful at first, then becomes the new normal.

His example: a painful five-minute daily workflow, flagged in interviews, surveys, support tickets and analytics. The team fixed it in a redesign — **time on task dropped to under two minutes** and error rates fell.

There was immediate positive feedback. Within a week, people had moved on.

try.q: What happened a week after the workflow was fixed?
options: People had moved on and treated it as normal
Usage of the feature dropped again
try.explain: The new design became the assumed baseline expectation.

learn.title: Why it feels like nothing happened
learn.text:
Once users stop thinking about the original pain points, the work that removed them **has nothing left to anchor to**.

And product teams forget the old version almost immediately. Once the new design stabilises, the comparison point disappears for everyone.

From the user's side it wasn't an improvement at all — it was fixing something that was broken.

try.q: Why does the improvement stop being visible?
options: The comparison point disappears for everyone
Metrics revert to their old levels over time
Users find new problems to report
try.explain: Nobody remembers the old version, so there is nothing to compare against.

learn.title: The reframe
learn.text:
Research has shown the thankless feeling doesn't come from a weakness in the field or a lack of appreciation. **It comes from how human adaptation works.**

So the fix isn't to chase recognition. It's to adjust expectations to reality — and to note that UX impact is **easier to measure in the moment than to feel later**, which is an argument for capturing the before-and-after while the comparison still exists.

try.q: What does the article say about measuring impact?
options: It is easier to measure in the moment than to feel later
It should be measured a quarter after launch
try.explain: Which is why you capture the comparison while it still exists.

options: Returning to a stable level of satisfaction after a change
Preferring familiar interfaces to new ones
Adjusting effort to the difficulty of a task
test.explain: It applies to positive and negative changes alike.

test.q: What happened to time on task in his example?
options: It dropped to under two minutes
It stayed about the same after the redesign
test.explain: From a painful five-minute workflow, with error rates falling too.

test.q: Where does the thankless feeling come from?
options: A lack of appreciation for UX
test.explain: Not a weakness in the field.

test.q: How does the user experience the improvement?
options: As a change they didn't ask for
As a reason to use the product more
test.explain: Which is why it generates no lasting credit.

test.q: What does the article suggest doing with the feeling?
test.explain: A lot of the stress around UX impact disappears with the reframe.
